newsitem.title: FRANCE: New supply fears drive up wheat prices.
newsitem.headline: New supply fears drive up wheat prices.

text.p: Wheat prices are jumping again as the weather turns against crops in key producing nations and heavy consumption slows a tentative recovery in world stocks.

Freezing weather in the Great Plains of the United States pushed U.S. wheat futures up by their daily limit in electronic dealing early on Monday, and similar gains were expected when Chicago opened for formal trading later in the day.
In France, hampered by early fears of drought after weeks without rain, prices for the crop to be harvested in three months' time rose up to three percent, grain dealers said.
In Australia futures prices for the next harvest added five percent on world supply concerns and dry weather at home.
"This is a pure weather market," a European trader said. "It is going to be rough like this for a few months."
Benchmark soft red winter wheat from the United States was indicated up by the 20 cents per bushel trading limit in Asian and early European trading at $4.28-1/4 per bushel for July.
That is worth around $162 per tonne on world markets, up from lows of around $140 per tonne seen earlier this year.
Wheat prices a year ago were peaking at record highs of $280 per tonne after a spate of previous droughts left global grain reserves at their lowest levels since a food scare in the 1970s.

But although several big grain nations including Australia and western Europe reaped record harvests in 1996, halving prices in a matter of months, the trend is in reverse yet again after much of the recovery was soaked up by strong demand.
"It's a lot tighter than envisaged at the start of the season," Steve Thornhill, director of market information at Britain's semi-public Home Grown Cereals Authority, said.
"The huge harvest has been absorbed better than expected," he said, citing increases in demand especially for animal feed.
Monday's price ignored fresh forecasts of another bumper grain harvest this year.
The United Nations' Rome-based Food and Agriculture Organisation said it expected record 1997 cereals production of 1,880 million tonnes, up from 1,873 million in 1996.
But with stockpiles managing only an awkward recovery, markets are once again having to pay attention to the weather.

The U.S. Agriculture Department (USDA) on Friday cut its key forecast for the amount of wheat held in storage at mid-year, just before the big northern hemisphere harvests start to arrive, by four million tonnes to 108 million tonnes.
"This is less than three million tonnes above the previous year's stocks. Remember what happened to wheat prices in that year," Geneva-based grain consultant James Dunsterville said.
At the same time, the USDA boosted its projections for 1996/97 global demand by some five million tonnes to 579 million and left last year's crop estimate almost steady at 581 million.
"This is going to be a year where the world harvest seems to be in trouble and demand is expanding," Dunsterville said.
London commodity broker GNI Ltd said demand was expected to carry on rising in the next 12 months and could tilt world wheat markets back into deficit even with good growing conditions.
Last year was the first time in four years that world output had exceeded demand, allowing some replenishment of stocks.
But traders warned against gambling too quickly on another drastic increase like last year's price explosion.
New wheat varieties are increasingly resistant to weather and France, Europe's top grain grower, had a record crop last year despite nearly identical drought fears in the spring.
